claims.claim: Abstaining on low-confidence inputs raises accuracy on the accepted set by a large, tunable margin: a VGG-16/ResNet-50 ImageNet classifier can be driven to 2% top-5 error on the answered subset while still answering about 59% of inputs, with the risk guaranteed at confidence 99.9%.
claims.locator: Abstract; Sec 1 (Introduction, contributions); Sec 5.3, Table 6 (ImageNet RESNET50 top-5)
claims.quote: For example, using our method an unprecedented 2% error in top-5 ImageNet classification can be guaranteed with probability 99.9%, and almost 60% test coverage.
claims.what_was_measured: Selective risk (0/1 error computed only over non-rejected test points) and coverage (fraction of test points not rejected), for a selective classifier built by thresholding the softmax-response (SR) confidence of a pretrained DNN.
claims.effect_size: ImageNet top-5, RESNET-50, target risk r*=0.02: test risk 0.0189 at test coverage 0.5935. Same setting with VGG-16: test risk 0.0179 at test coverage 0.5351. Compare the full-coverage baseline: the paper's ImageNet top-5 error at coverage 1.0 is roughly 8-10% (read off the risk-coverage curve, Figure 2c), so abstaining on ~40% of inputs cuts error on the answered subset by roughly 4-5x.
claims.sample: ImageNet ILSVRC2014; the validation set split in two, giving SGR training and held-out test sets of approximately 25,000 examples each. delta = 0.001.
claims.limits: The paper states it studies only the 0/1 loss and does not control false-positive/false-negative rates separately: 'In this paper we only studied selective classification under the 0/1 loss. It would be of great importance to extend our techniques to other loss functions and specifically to regression, and to fully control false-positive and false-negative rates.' All guarantees assume the calibration/test data are sampled i.i.d. from the same distribution P; no distribution shift is considered. It also does not train the classifier and the rejector jointly - that is named as the main open question.
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: On CIFAR-10 the same method reaches 1% error on the answered subset while still answering more than 78% of inputs, against a base model with about 6.5% error at full coverage.
claims.locator: Sec 5.1 (Selective Guaranteed Risk for CIFAR-10), text following Table 1
claims.quote: Finally, we see that it is possible to guarantee with this method amazingly small 1% error while covering more than 78% of the domain.
claims.what_was_measured: Test selective risk and test coverage of a VGG-16 CIFAR-10 model under the SGR (Selection with Guaranteed Risk) thresholding procedure, for a sweep of target risks r*.
claims.effect_size: Target r*=0.01 -> test risk 0.0092 at test coverage 0.7856. Base model full-coverage validation accuracy 93.54% (i.e. ~6.46% error). So error on the accepted set falls ~7x (6.46% -> 0.92%) at the cost of rejecting ~21% of inputs. The rest of the sweep: r*=0.02 -> 0.0149 risk / 0.8466 coverage; r*=0.03 -> 0.0261 / 0.8966; r*=0.04 -> 0.0380 / 0.9318; r*=0.05 -> 0.0486 / 0.9596; r*=0.06 -> 0.0572 / 0.9784.
claims.sample: CIFAR-10 standard validation set randomly split in two halves of approximately 5,000 examples each: one for SGR threshold selection, one held out for testing. delta = 0.001.
claims.limits: Same as C1 - i.i.d. assumption, 0/1 loss only. The paper additionally notes it did not apply a Bonferroni correction across the 6-7 target-risk rows per table: 'With this small delta, and small number of reported experiments (6-7 lines in each table) we did not perform a Bonferroni correction (which can be easily added).' The baseline error figure (93.54% accuracy) is a validation accuracy reported in prose, not a matched full-coverage row of the same table.
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: A decline threshold can be selected against a stated risk target with a high-probability guarantee: choosing the threshold on a calibration set with a binomial-tail bound produced test risk at or below the bound in every reported run.
claims.locator: Sec 5.1, text following Table 1; Algorithm 1 (SGR) and Theorem/Lemma in Sec 3
claims.quote: Observing the results in Table 1, we see that the risk bound, b*, is always very close to the the target risk, r*. Moreover, the test risk is always bounded above by the bound b*, as required.
claims.what_was_measured: Whether the empirically measured test risk of the selected threshold respects the target risk r* and the numerical bound b* returned by the SGR procedure, across a sweep of r* values and three datasets.
claims.effect_size: Every reported row satisfies test risk <= b*. CIFAR-10: r*=0.01 -> b*=0.0099, test risk 0.0092. CIFAR-100: r*=0.05 -> b*=0.0499, test risk 0.0413 at coverage 0.4450. ImageNet VGG-16 top-1: r*=0.10 -> b*=0.1000, test risk 0.0948 at coverage 0.5951. Bounds hold across 6-7 target levels x 6 tables (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet top-1/top-5 for VGG-16 and RESNET-50).
claims.sample: CIFAR-10 (~5,000 calibration / ~5,000 test), CIFAR-100 (same design), ImageNet (~25,000 / ~25,000), delta = 0.001.
claims.limits: The guarantee is a high-probability statement over an i.i.d. calibration draw, not a per-input guarantee, and holds only under the same-distribution assumption. No Bonferroni correction was applied across the multiple target-risk rows. The bound is proved for a fixed pretrained classifier f and a given confidence-rate function; the paper does not claim optimality of the rejection mechanism ('it might be possible to identify superior mechanisms for a given classifier f').
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: Raw softmax confidence from a modern deep network is NOT calibrated: the network's stated confidence systematically exceeds its accuracy, and the gap grows with model capacity even as accuracy improves.
claims.locator: Sec 1 (Introduction), Figure 1; Sec 5.2 / Table 1 (ECE before and after calibration); Sec 6 (Conclusion)
claims.quote: While neural networks today are undoubtedly more accurate than they were a decade ago, we discover with great surprise that modern neural networks are no longer well-calibrated.
claims.what_was_measured: Expected Calibration Error (ECE, with M=15 equal-width confidence bins) of the maximum-softmax confidence, plus reliability diagrams (accuracy as a function of confidence), before and after post-hoc calibration.
claims.effect_size: Uncalibrated ECE, CIFAR-100 / ResNet-110: 16.53%, falling to 1.26% under temperature scaling. Other uncalibrated ECEs from the same table: CIFAR-100 Wide ResNet 32 15.0%; CIFAR-100 ResNet 110 (SD) 12.67%; CIFAR-100 DenseNet 40 10.37%; Birds/ResNet-50 9.19%; ImageNet DenseNet 161 6.28%, ResNet 152 5.48%; CIFAR-10 ResNet 110 4.6%; CIFAR-100 LeNet 5 only 4.85%. The old shallow LeNet 5 on CIFAR-10 is 3.02%. Figure 1 contrasts a 5-layer LeNet (error 44.9% on CIFAR-100, confidence roughly matching accuracy) with a 110-layer ResNet (error 30.6%, confidence far above accuracy).
claims.sample: Eight datasets x multiple architectures: Birds, Cars, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, SVHN (vision) and 20 News, Reuters, SST Binary, SST Fine Grained (NLP); 19 dataset-model rows in Table 1.
claims.limits: The paper says explicitly that it does not explain the mechanism: 'It remains future work to understand why these trends affect calibration while improving accuracy.' It also flags that its own measurements may be binning- or split-dependent: 'It is also possible that our measurements are affected by dataset split or by the particular binning scheme.' One dataset (Reuters) was already well calibrated (ECE <= 1%) and temperature scaling did not help there. ECE is an aggregate over bins and can mask which bins are wrong. No abstention experiment is run: the paper measures calibration, not coverage/risk.
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: The plain-language reading of calibration - '90% confident means 90% correct' - is the paper's own definition, and it states perfect calibration is unattainable in practice.
claims.quote: We would like the confidence estimate P to be calibrated, which intuitively means that P represents a true probability. For example, given 100 predictions, each with confidence of 0.8, we expect that 80 should be correctly classified.
claims.what_was_measured: Definitional, not an experiment. Perfect calibration is formalised as P(Yhat = Y | Phat = p) = p for all p in [0,1]; ECE and reliability diagrams are the finite-sample approximations used everywhere else in the paper.
claims.effect_size: Not applicable - a definition. Directly quoted caveat from the same paragraph: 'In all practical settings, achieving perfect calibration is impossible.'
claims.limits: The paper notes the calibration probability 'cannot be computed using finitely many samples since Phat is a continuous random variable' - hence all reported calibration numbers are binned estimates, not the quantity in the definition.
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: A model's raw max-softmax probability means different things on in-distribution and out-of-distribution inputs: at the same nominal confidence, the true correctness rate can differ by tens of points, so one threshold fitted in-domain is wrong once traffic shifts.
claims.locator: Sec 5.3 (Overconfidence of MaxProb), text discussing Figures 3a-3d
claims.quote: Figure 3b shows that MaxProb is not well calibrated: it is underconfident in-domain, and overconfident out-of-domain. For example, for a MaxProb of 0.6, the model is about 80% likely to get the question correct if it came from SQuAD (in-domain), and 45% likely to get the question correct if it was OOD.
claims.what_was_measured: True probability of correctness (exact-match correctness of the BERT extractive QA answer) plotted against MaxProb (the model's maximum softmax probability over answer spans), separately for in-domain and out-of-domain examples.
claims.effect_size: At MaxProb = 0.6, correctness is about 80% in-domain versus about 45% OOD - a ~35 point spread at identical stated confidence. Downstream consequence measured in Table 1: MaxProb yields only 48.23% coverage at an 80% accuracy target and 21.07% coverage at a 90% target, on the mixed test stream.
claims.sample: BERT-base QA model trained on SQuAD; five OOD QA datasets (TriviaQA, HotpotQA, NewsQA, Natural Questions, SearchQA); results averaged over 20 (known-OOD, unknown-OOD) dataset pairings and 10 random data splits; test stream is a uniform mixture of SQuAD and unknown-OOD questions.
claims.limits: The paper states the in-domain underconfidence is an artifact of SQuAD's single-answer training versus multi-answer evaluation, and that removing multiple answers makes MaxProb well calibrated in-domain while it 'stays overconfident out-of-domain'. It also draws a boundary on what the finding implies: 'Note that miscalibration out-of-domain does not imply poor selective prediction on OOD data, but does imply poor selective prediction in our mixture setting.' Single model family (BERT), single task type (extractive QA).
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: Selecting the decline threshold against an explicit accuracy (precision) target is a measurable design choice, and what confidence signal you threshold changes how much you can auto-answer at that target: a trained error-predicting calibrator answered 56.1% of questions at 80% accuracy where raw model probability answered only 48.2%.
claims.locator: Abstract; Sec 1 (Introduction, results summary); Sec 5.2 and Table 1
claims.quote: On average, the trained calibrator achieves 56.1% coverage (i.e., the system answers 56.1% of test questions) while maintaining 80% accuracy on answered questions, outperforming MaxProb with the same QA model (48.2% coverage at 80% accuracy), using MaxProb and training the QA model on both SQuAD and the known OOD data (51.8% coverage), and training the calibrator only on SQuAD data (53.7% coverage).
claims.what_was_measured: Coverage at a fixed accuracy target (Cov@Acc=80% and Cov@Acc=90%) - i.e. the threshold is set so accuracy on answered questions hits the target, and the fraction answered is the score. Also AUC of the risk-coverage curve (lower better).
claims.effect_size: Cov@Acc=80%: MaxProb 48.23 -> calibrator (p_source and q_known) 56.06 (+7.8 points); Cov@Acc=90%: 21.07 -> 29.42 (+8.4 points); risk-coverage AUC 20.54 -> 18.47. Against the stronger baseline of a QA model retrained on SQuAD + known OOD and thresholded by MaxProb, the gain is '4.3 points and 6.7 points higher coverage at 80% and 90% accuracy respectively, and 1.1 points lower AUC' (95% CI for the AUC gap [1.01, 1.69], paired bootstrap, 1000 samples). Adding test-time dropout features lifts the calibrator to 59.99 Cov@Acc=80%.
claims.sample: 1,600 SQuAD + 1,600 known-OOD examples for calibrator training, 400+400 for hyperparameter validation; averaged over 20 OOD dataset pairings and 10 random splits. Calibrator is a random forest over features derived from the input and the QA model's softmax outputs.
claims.limits: The paper reports a large residual gap to the oracle: 'Best possible' coverage with the same base model is 74.92 at Acc=80% and 66.59 at Acc=90%, versus 56.06 / 29.42 achieved - and it adds that 'achieving this bound may not be realistic.' It also states the finding is conditional on not having samples of the actual test-time OOD distribution: 'We note that our findings do not hold in the alternate setting where we have access to samples from q_unk (instead of q_known).' Error analysis found many apparent overconfidence errors were span-mismatch/valid-alternate-answer artifacts ('62% of overconfidence errors are due to the model predicting valid alternate answers, or span mismatches'), so the measured accuracy is a lower bound on true correctness.
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: LLM self-reported (verbalized) confidence is badly miscalibrated and systematically overconfident: stated confidences pile up in the 80-100% band in multiples of 5 while accuracy in those bins is far lower.
claims.locator: Sec 5.1 (LLMs tend to be overconfident when verbalizing their confidence); Figure 2 caption; Table 2
claims.quote: According to the criteria given in Srivastava et al. (2023), GPT-3, GPT-3.5, and Vicuna exhibit notably high ECE values, e.g., the average ECE exceeding 0.377, suggesting that the verbalized confidence of these LLMs are poorly calibrated. While GPT-4 displays lower ECE, its AUROC and AUPRC-Negative scores remain suboptimal, with an average AUROC of merely 62.7%—close to the 50% random guess threshold—highlighting challenges in distinguishing correct from incorrect predictions.
claims.what_was_measured: ECE of the model's verbalized confidence (elicited by prompting the model to state a confidence number), and failure-prediction quality measured as AUROC / AUPRC-Positive / AUPRC-Negative of that confidence as a score for correct-vs-incorrect.
claims.effect_size: Average ECE > 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna (the paper's threshold for 'significant deviation' is ECE > 0.25). GPT-4's average AUROC for separating its own correct from incorrect answers is 62.7% (chance = 50%). Scaling helps but does not fix it: 'approximate 22.2% improvement in AUROC from GPT-3 to GPT-4.' Figure 2 caption: 'the confidence levels primarily range between 80% and 100%, often in multiples of 5; 2) the accuracy within each bin is much lower than its corresponding confidence, indicating significant overconfidence.'
claims.sample: Five LLMs (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna, LLaMA 2 Chat) x eight datasets across five task types (commonsense reasoning: SportUND, StrategyQA; arithmetic: GSM8K, SVAMP; symbolic: DateUnd, ObjectCou; professional knowledge: MMLU Professional Law; ethics: MMLU Business Ethics).
claims.limits: The paper's own Limitations paragraph restricts scope: 'We mainly focuses on fixed-form and free-form question-answering QA tasks where the ground truth answer is unique, while leaving tasks such as summarization and open-ended QA to the future work' and notes the black-box setting is a deliberate restriction, with white-box (logit) methods performing better (AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605 in their comparison). Results are tied to specific 2023-era model snapshots and to the specific elicitation prompts in their Table 14.
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: A good calibration score is NOT sufficient to justify a confidence threshold: a model can score near-optimal ECE while emitting a single constant confidence, leaving zero ability to separate its correct from incorrect answers - so ECE must be read together with a discrimination metric such as AUROC.
claims.locator: Sec 5.2 (Human-inspired prompting strategies partially reduce overconfidence)
claims.quote: For example, with the CoT prompting on the GSM8K dataset, GPT-4 with 93.6% accuracy achieves a near-optimal ECE 0.064 by assigning 100% confidence to all samples. However, since all samples receive the same confidence, it is challenging to distinguish between correct and incorrect samples based on the verbalized confidence.
claims.what_was_measured: ECE versus AUROC of the same verbalized-confidence signal under five prompting strategies (vanilla, CoT, Multi-Step, Top-K, Self-Probing) across five datasets and two models.
claims.effect_size: GPT-4 + CoT on GSM8K: accuracy 93.6%, ECE 0.064 (near-optimal) produced entirely by a degenerate constant confidence of 100% - so AUROC is at or near chance for that configuration. Generally: 'while we can reduce ECE with the right prompting strategy, the model's failure prediction capability is still limited, i.e., close to the performance of random guess (AUROC=0.5).'
claims.sample: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 x five datasets x five prompting strategies (Figure 3 / Table 10).
claims.limits: The paper states the reliability caveat itself: 'The reliability of the given confidence must be assessed by considering multiple metrics, such as both ECE and AUROC. As discussed in section 5.2, a high ECE does not imply that the model's outputs accurately represent model correctness.' The degenerate-constant case is illustrated on one model/dataset pairing; the paper does not quantify how often the degeneracy occurs. It also does not run a coverage/risk abstention experiment - it measures calibration and failure prediction, not deployed abstention rates.
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: A distribution-free procedure exists for picking the decline threshold against a stated accuracy target: scan the confidence cutoff using a binomial upper confidence bound on the selective error and take the smallest cutoff whose bound stays under alpha - the resulting threshold satisfies the selective-accuracy target with probability 1 - delta.
claims.locator: Sec 5.5 (Selective Classification), Equations (15) and the two display equations following it, Proposition 4
claims.quote: This is called a selective accuracy guarantee, because the accuracy is only computed over a subset of high-confidence predictions. This quantity cannot be controlled with techniques we’ve seen so far, since we are not guaranteed that model accuracy is monotone in the cutoff λ. Nonetheless, it can be handled with Learn then Test—a framework for controlling arbitrary risks (see Appendix A).
claims.what_was_measured: Selective accuracy P(Ytest = Yhat(Xtest) | Phat(Xtest) >= λ-hat) >= 1 - alpha, with λ-hat chosen on a calibration set; the empirical demonstration is accuracy versus fraction-kept on ImageNet at alpha = 0.1.
claims.effect_size: NO in-text numeric effect size. The paper's own words for the guarantee are: 'Proposition 4. Assume the {(Xi, Yi)}n i=1 and (Xtest, Ytest) are i.i.d. and λ-hat is chosen as above. Then (15) is satisfied with probability 1 - delta.' The empirical result is delegated entirely to a figure - 'See results on Imagenet at level alpha = 0.1 in Figure 17' - whose axes are accuracy versus fraction kept. I did not extract numeric values from that figure and will not invent them.
claims.sample: ImageNet, alpha = 0.1; calibration-set size not stated in this section (the tutorial's running examples use on the order of 500-1000 calibration points). Sample details live in the accompanying notebook, which I did not open.
claims.limits: The guarantee is MARGINAL, not per-input. The paper is explicit: conditional coverage 'is a stronger property than the marginal coverage property in (1) that conformal prediction is guaranteed to achieve—indeed, in the most general case, conditional coverage is impossible to achieve [14]. In other words, conformal procedures are not guaranteed to satisfy (7), so we must check how close our procedure comes to approximating it.' It also requires i.i.d./exchangeable calibration and test data - a threshold set this way carries no guarantee under distribution shift unless the weighted/covariate-shift variants are used - and the coverage realised on any ONE fixed calibration set fluctuates around 1 - alpha rather than equalling it.
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

claims.claim: Marginal coverage/risk guarantees permit all the errors to land in one subgroup, so a threshold that meets a global precision target can still be badly wrong for a specific slice of traffic.
claims.locator: Sec 3 (Evaluating conformal prediction / Conditional coverage), text around Equation (7) and Figure 10
claims.quote: This is a stronger property than the marginal coverage property in (1) that conformal prediction is guaranteed to achieve—indeed, in the most general case, conditional coverage is impossible to achieve [14]. In other words, conformal procedures are not guaranteed to satisfy (7), so we must check how close our procedure comes to approximating it.
claims.what_was_measured: Conceptual/theoretical, with two proposed diagnostics: feature-stratified coverage (FSC) and size-stratified coverage, each measuring realised coverage within a stratum and comparing it to 1 - alpha.
claims.effect_size: No effect size - this is an impossibility statement plus a diagnostic recipe. The paper's worked illustration: two groups at 90% and 10% frequency where prediction sets always cover in the large group and never in the small one still satisfy 90% marginal coverage.
claims.limits: The tutorial does not itself measure how large a slice-level violation is in practice for the selective-classification procedure of Sec 5.5; it supplies metrics for the practitioner to check on their own data. It cites [87], [88] for the precise conditions under which distribution-free conditional guarantees can exist.
claims.verified_by: coordinator re-fetched the PDF and re-extracted with pdfminer; 9 of 11 quotes matched verbatim after de-hyphenation, the other 2 differ only by a footnote marker and a lost ff ligature in MY extraction

expected_failure: Asked where to put the decline threshold, the baseline reasons about the tradeoff in prose and picks a round number, without deriving it from the score distribution against a stated precision target, and without reporting what coverage that number costs.

route uncertain cases to a human
what precision can we ship at

representative_tasks.task: Our extraction model is confidently wrong on about one record in twenty and a human reviews everything. Where do we put the auto-approve cut?
representative_tasks.artifact_expected: A threshold derived from the score distribution against a named precision target, with the coverage it buys stated.

representative_tasks.task: Here are 200 scored predictions with labels. Pick the cut for a 95 percent precision target.
representative_tasks.artifact_expected: The cut, the achieved precision and the coverage at that cut, computed from the data rather than asserted.

representative_tasks.task: Can we just auto-approve everything the model says it is 90 percent sure about?
representative_tasks.artifact_expected: A refusal that turns on whether the reported confidence is calibrated, not on the number being too low.

threshold: Across k >= 2 repeats: zero regressions on correctness, no more than 20 percent worse on tokens or tool calls, and at least one test where the skill wins with the win surviving the repeat.
